body:
What is an artificial satellite?

A satellite is an object that revolves around a larger celestial body under the influence of gravity. The Moon is a natural satellite of Earth. An artificial satellite is a human-made object placed in orbit for purposes such as communication, Earth observation, weather monitoring, navigation or scientific study.

A satellite does not have to be directly above one country or remain above the same place. Its position relative to Earth's surface depends on the orbit selected for its mission.

An orbit is the path followed by a body around another body under the influence of gravity. An artificial Earth satellite follows an orbit because of the combined effects of Earth's gravitational attraction and the satellite's motion.

Why does a satellite remain in orbit?

Earth attracts objects towards its centre through gravity. If a ball is dropped, it falls towards the ground. A satellite is also attracted by Earth, but it has enough sideways motion to keep moving around the planet instead of falling directly onto its surface.

In a circular orbit, the satellite continuously changes its direction of motion. This change requires an inward acceleration, which is supplied by Earth's gravitational force. The inward force is called the centripetal force. Thus, gravity provides the centripetal force necessary for orbital motion.

Consider a satellite moving along a circular path. At any instant, its tendency to continue moving is along a tangent to the orbit, while gravity acts approximately towards Earth's centre. Together, these produce a curved orbital path.

In an ideal circular orbit, the satellite may have a constant speed even though its velocity changes continuously. This is because velocity includes both speed and direction. A change in direction is sufficient to produce acceleration.

Does a satellite need continuous rocket thrust?

No. Once a satellite has entered a suitable orbit, it does not need to keep firing its engine simply to move around Earth. Its existing motion and Earth's gravity maintain the orbit. Small propulsion systems may nevertheless be used occasionally to correct the orbit, compensate for disturbances or maintain a required position.

Satellites in very low orbits also experience some atmospheric drag. Over time, this can reduce their altitude unless corrections are made. The amount of correction needed depends on the satellite and its orbit.

Gravity does not disappear in space. Orbiting astronauts and satellites experience apparent weightlessness mainly because they are in continuous free fall around Earth, not because Earth has stopped attracting them.

Basic terms used to describe an orbit

An orbit can be described by its altitude, shape, inclination and orbital period.

  • Altitude: The satellite's height above Earth's surface. A higher altitude generally means a larger orbital path.
  • Orbital period: The time required to complete 1 revolution around Earth.
  • Inclination: The angle between the satellite's orbital plane and Earth's equatorial plane.
  • Circular orbit: An orbit in which the satellite's distance from Earth's centre remains approximately constant.
  • Elliptical orbit: An elongated orbit in which the satellite's distance from Earth changes.

For an elliptical Earth orbit, the point nearest Earth is called the perigee, while the farthest point is called the apogee. These terms become important when studying transfer orbits used during satellite launches.

Revolution and rotation are different

Revolution refers to the movement of a satellite around Earth. Rotation refers to the turning of an object about its own axis. A satellite may revolve around Earth while also adjusting its own orientation to keep an antenna or camera pointed in the required direction.

Earth itself rotates about its axis and revolves around the Sun. These motions are distinct from the revolution of an artificial satellite around Earth.

Prelims focus

  • The Moon is a natural satellite; an Earth-observation spacecraft is an artificial satellite.
  • Earth's gravitational attraction provides the centripetal force for orbital motion.
  • A satellite in a circular orbit changes direction continuously, even if its speed remains constant.
  • Orbital period means the time for 1 complete revolution.
  • Perigee is the nearest point and apogee is the farthest point of an elliptical Earth orbit.
  • Trap: An orbiting satellite does not require continuous rocket thrust, and gravity is not absent in orbit.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 9, 2018–19 edition, Chapter 8, 'Motion', sections 8.5–8.6, pp. 107–111; Chapter 10, 'Gravitation', section 10.1, pp. 131–134. NCERT, The Earth: Our Habitat, Class 6, 2018–19 edition, Chapter 3, 'Motions of the Earth', pp. 18–21. European Space Agency, 'Types of orbits', introductory discussion and 'Transfer orbits and Geostationary Transfer Orbit' sections, published 30 March 2020; consulted 4 November 2026.]

body:
Why does orbital altitude matter?

The altitude of a satellite determines how far it is from Earth, how quickly it travels around the planet and how much of Earth's surface it can see at once. These factors influence the choice of orbit for communication, navigation, imaging and weather observation.

For an approximately circular Earth orbit, satellites at lower altitudes generally move faster and complete a revolution in less time than satellites in higher orbits. A satellite at a greater height can usually view a larger area at once, but it is also farther from the people and places it observes or communicates with.

The 3 major altitude categories

OrbitAltitude and motionCommon applications
Low Earth Orbit (LEO)Generally below 2,000 km; a typical low-orbit satellite completes a revolution in about 90 minutes.Earth imaging, scientific missions, space stations and satellite communication constellations.
Medium Earth Orbit (MEO)Above the LEO region and below the geostationary altitude; orbital periods are longer than those of typical LEO satellites.Many satellite navigation systems, including Galileo.
Geostationary Earth Orbit (GEO)Approximately 35,786 km above the equator; the satellite appears fixed over one longitude.Telecommunications, broadcasting and continuous weather observation of a region.

These categories are broad descriptions of orbital regions. A satellite's actual mission also depends on its inclination, instruments, communication system and other orbital characteristics.

Low Earth Orbit: close to the planet

LEO is especially useful for observing Earth's surface. A camera closer to Earth can generally capture finer surface details than an otherwise similar camera at a much greater distance. Many Earth-observation satellites therefore operate in low orbits.

Satellites in LEO travel quickly around Earth. A typical low-orbit satellite moves at approximately 7.8 km per second and completes an orbit in roughly 90 minutes. The International Space Station also operates in LEO.

A single low-orbit satellite usually passes within view of a particular ground station for only a limited period. It then moves beyond the station's view. Consequently, communication services requiring extensive, nearly continuous coverage commonly use constellations, meaning groups of satellites operating together.

Lower distance can reduce communication delay. However, the shorter viewing period of an individual satellite creates a need for suitable ground-station arrangements or multiple satellites.

Medium Earth Orbit: useful for navigation

MEO lies between the low-orbit region and geostationary altitude. Satellites in this region take longer to complete each revolution than typical LEO satellites and can cover larger areas from a single position.

MEO is widely used for Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS). In such systems, a receiver uses timed signals from multiple satellites to determine its position. Europe's Galileo navigation system is an example of a system using MEO satellites.

However, MEO is not a compulsory orbit for every navigation system. India's NavIC system is an important exception, because its published constellation design uses geostationary and inclined geosynchronous satellites.

Geostationary Earth Orbit: fixed relative to the ground

A satellite in GEO revolves in a circular orbit above the equator in the same direction as Earth's rotation, taking exactly 1 sidereal day to complete an orbit. Its period is approximately 23 hours, 56 minutes and 4 seconds. This is different from the ordinary solar day of 24 hours.

Because the satellite's angular motion matches Earth's rotation, it appears to remain over the same point on the equator. A ground antenna communicating with such a satellite can generally remain pointed in a fixed direction.

GEO is useful for telecommunications, television broadcasting and continuous observation of large weather systems. Its considerable height permits a broad view of Earth, although a single GEO satellite cannot see the whole planet. Coverage is also less favourable towards the poles because Earth blocks or reduces the viewing angle towards high-latitude regions.

Signals must travel a much greater distance between the ground and a GEO satellite than between the ground and a LEO satellite. This increases communication delay. Thus, GEO offers wide, persistent regional coverage, while LEO offers a shorter signal path and often better conditions for detailed imaging.

LEO: closer view and rapid revolutions. MEO: commonly used for global navigation constellations. GEO: persistent view of the same broad region. These are common uses, not exclusive functions.

Choosing the orbit for a task

Suppose a mission must produce detailed images of agricultural fields. A relatively low orbit may be suitable because the satellite is close enough to observe surface features effectively. If a mission must continuously observe cloud development over a large region, GEO is often useful because the satellite keeps viewing that region.

A communication service may choose either GEO or a constellation of low-orbit satellites. The choice depends on coverage, delay, the number of satellites required and the intended service. Orbit selection is a trade-off, not a rule that one orbit is universally better.

Prelims focus

  • LEO generally extends to altitudes below 2,000 km.
  • A typical low-orbit satellite takes about 90 minutes to complete 1 revolution.
  • MEO is commonly used for navigation constellations such as Galileo.
  • GEO is about 35,786 km above Earth's equator.
  • A GEO satellite completes 1 revolution in approximately 23 hours, 56 minutes and 4 seconds.
  • Trap: Not every communication satellite is in GEO, and not every navigation satellite is in MEO.

[Sources: European Space Agency, 'Types of orbits', sections 'Low Earth orbit (LEO)', 'Medium Earth orbit (MEO)' and 'Geostationary orbit (GEO)', published 30 March 2020; consulted 4 November 2026. Indian Space Research Organisation, 'Satellite Navigation Services', section 'Navigation with Indian Constellation (NavIC)'; consulted 4 November 2026.]

body:
Altitude and inclination describe different things

An orbit can be classified by more than 1 characteristic. Altitude describes the satellite's height. Inclination describes how its orbital plane is tilted relative to Earth's equatorial plane. The shape of the path and its period provide additional information.

For example, a satellite can be both in LEO and in a polar orbit. These labels do not conflict: LEO describes its height, while polar describes the direction of its orbital plane.

Equatorial and polar orbits

An equatorial orbit lies in Earth's equatorial plane and has an inclination of approximately 0° when it travels in the direction of Earth's rotation.

A polar orbit passes over or near Earth's polar regions. Its inclination is approximately 90°. Such an orbit runs broadly north–south rather than following the equator.

As a polar-orbiting satellite circles Earth, Earth rotates beneath its orbital plane. On successive revolutions the satellite passes over different longitudes. Over time, this permits observation of much of Earth's surface, including high-latitude areas.

Polar orbits are commonly used for Earth observation, environmental monitoring and mapping. They are often low Earth orbits, although the word polar itself identifies orbital inclination rather than a fixed altitude.

Sun-synchronous orbit: comparable lighting conditions

A Sun-Synchronous Orbit (SSO) is a special near-polar orbit arranged so that the satellite passes over a given location at approximately the same local solar time on successive visits. This produces broadly similar Sun positions and lighting conditions when images are taken.

For example, if the satellite observes an agricultural region at approximately the same local solar time on successive passes, the resulting photographs are easier to compare. Differences caused simply by the Sun being at a very different position are reduced.

SSO is especially useful for studying vegetation, land use, forest cover and environmental change. Many Sun-synchronous satellites operate at altitudes of roughly 600–800 km, although this is a common range rather than a definition.

A Sun-synchronous satellite is not stationary above a place. It continues moving around Earth. The defining feature is the approximately consistent local solar time of its observations, not a fixed position over the ground.

Geosynchronous and geostationary are not identical

A Geosynchronous Orbit (GSO) is an orbit whose period matches Earth's rotation period relative to the stars: approximately 23 hours, 56 minutes and 4 seconds.

A satellite in GSO need not appear fixed in the sky. If its orbit is inclined or elliptical, its apparent position changes during the day even though its orbital period matches Earth's rotation.

A Geostationary Earth Orbit (GEO) is a particular type of geosynchronous orbit that meets all the following conditions:

  • It is circular.
  • It lies directly above the equator.
  • It moves from west to east, in the direction of Earth's rotation.
  • Its orbital period equals Earth's sidereal rotation period.

When these conditions are satisfied, the satellite appears fixed over one longitude. Therefore, every geostationary orbit is geosynchronous, but not every geosynchronous orbit is geostationary.

Indian example: NavIC

Navigation with Indian Constellation (NavIC) is India's regional satellite navigation system, previously known as the Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System (IRNSS).

ISRO's published NavIC system design specifies a constellation of 7 satellites: 3 geostationary satellites and 4 inclined geosynchronous satellites. The inclined geosynchronous component is designed with an inclination of approximately 29°.

This is an important application of the distinction between GEO and GSO. The 7-satellite description refers to the published constellation design; it should not be interpreted as a statement that all 7 satellites are operational at a particular date.

Geostationary Transfer Orbit: a path to the final orbit

A Geostationary Transfer Orbit (GTO) is an elliptical orbit used to help a satellite reach its intended geostationary region. It is a transfer orbit, not the same thing as the final GEO.

A launcher may first place a satellite into GTO, with a low perigee and a much higher apogee near geostationary altitude. The satellite then uses its own propulsion system to raise and circularise its orbit and, where necessary, adjust its orbital inclination.

The distinction is visible in the names: GTO describes an intermediate path used to reach a higher orbit; GSO describes an orbital period matching Earth's rotation; and GEO describes the special circular, equatorial, Earth-synchronous orbit in which the satellite appears stationary.

Prelims focus

  • Equatorial orbit: inclination approximately 0° when moving in the direction of Earth's rotation.
  • Polar orbit: inclination approximately 90°; useful for broad Earth coverage over successive passes.
  • SSO: a near-polar orbit giving approximately the same local solar time of observation.
  • GSO: orbital period equal to Earth's sidereal rotation period.
  • NavIC's published 7-satellite design combines 3 GEO and 4 inclined GSO satellites.
  • Trap: GSO, GEO and GTO are not interchangeable terms.

[Sources: European Space Agency, 'Types of orbits', sections 'Polar orbit (PO)', 'Sun synchronous orbit (SSO)', 'Geostationary orbit (GEO)' and 'Transfer orbits and Geostationary Transfer Orbit (GTO)', published 30 March 2020; consulted 4 November 2026. Indian Space Research Organisation, 'Satellite Navigation Services', section 'Navigation with Indian Constellation (NavIC)'; consulted 4 November 2026. Indian Space Research Organisation, 'Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle Mark II', section 'CUS (Third Stage)'; consulted 4 November 2026.]
